record.original_question: Let Δ ⊂ TM be a bracket-generating distribution defining a sub-Riemannian structure on a manifold M, and let γ0, γ1 : [0,1] → M be smooth admissible paths with the same starting point q0 and linearly independent initial velocities at q0. Must there always exist an admissible path from γ0(1) to γ1(1) whose length is strictly less than the length of the broken path obtained by concatenating γ0 and γ1?

evidence.quote: Does there exist an admissible path connecting γ0(1) with γ1(1) that is strictly shorter than the concatenation of the curves γ0 and γ1?

Any improvement of the estimates for m and n would be very interesting. We still know very little about sub-Riemannian structures with big m and it may happen that the answer is negative for some m and n.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a smooth manifold equipped with a sub-Riemannian structure given by a bracket-generating distribution $\Delta \subset TM$ together with a smoothly varying inner product on $\Delta$. An absolutely continuous path $\gamma:[0,1]\to M$ is called admissible if $\dot\gamma(t) \in \Delta_{\gamma(t)}$ for almost every $t$, and its length is $\ell(\gamma) = \int_0^1 \|\dot\gamma(t)\|\,dt$. 

Suppose $\gamma_0,\gamma_1:[0,1]\to M$ are two smooth admissible paths sharing the common starting point $\gamma_0(0)=\gamma_1(0)=q_0$, and such that the initial velocities $\dot\gamma_0(0)$ and $\dot\gamma_1(0)$ are linearly independent vectors in $\Delta_{q_0}$. Consider the broken concatenation that follows $\gamma_0$ in reverse from $\gamma_0(1)$ to $q_0$ and then follows $\gamma_1$ from $q_0$ to $\gamma_1(1)$; its length equals $\ell(\gamma_0)+\ell(\gamma_1)$.

Prove or disprove: there always exists an admissible path from $\gamma_0(1)$ to $\gamma_1(1)$ whose length is strictly less than $\ell(\gamma_0)+\ell(\gamma_1)$.
artifact.status_search_result: The "cutting corners" question is affirmatively resolved by the theorem of Hakavuori and Le Donne (Inventiones Math. 206 (2016), 693–704), which proves that in any sub-Riemannian manifold a length-minimizing curve cannot contain a corner (a point where left and right tangent vectors are linearly independent admissible vectors). Consequently, the broken concatenation described, having a corner at $q_0$, is not length-minimizing between its endpoints, so a strictly shorter admissible connection between $\gamma_0(1)$ and $\gamma_1(1)$ always exists.

status_evidence.title: Non-minimality of corners in subriemannian geometry
status_evidence.snippet: We give a short solution to one of the main open problems in subriemannian geometry: length minimizers do not have corner-type singularities. With this result we solve Problem II of Agrachev's list.
status_evidence.claim: Hakavuori–Le Donne prove corners are never length-minimizing in sub-Riemannian geometry, resolving the cutting-corners problem.

status_evidence.title: Non-minimality of corners in subriemannian geometry (PDF)
status_evidence.snippet: Length minimizers in subriemannian manifolds do not have corner-type singularities.
status_evidence.claim: Direct theorem: a path with a corner is not minimizing, so a strictly shorter admissible path exists between its endpoints.
